name: Coloring (contrast / complexion) maxxing

lead: Coloring maxxing treats the face as a set of light and dark elements: iris against sclera, brows and lashes against skin, teeth against lips, hair against complexion. The idea is that clearer, more distinct contrasts make the face look alert, healthy and defined, and that people can adjust them through grooming, skincare, dyeing, makeup and clothing.

There is real research behind part of this. Perception studies by Richard Russell and colleagues found that luminance contrast between facial features and surrounding skin differs between men and women, and that makeup raises it in female faces. Forum guides go further, with colour typologies and rules of thumb that have not been tested.

paras: Common routes in forum guides include whitening teeth, reducing eye redness and dullness for brighter sclera, shaping or tinting brows and lashes, evening skin tone and treating dark circles, choosing a hair colour relative to eye and skin colour, and picking clothing colours that contrast with or flatter the complexion. Many of these are cosmetic or grooming steps that show results as soon as they are applied.

Most coloring steps are low-risk grooming, but individual methods carry their own risks, such as irritation from bleaching or dye products and sun damage from tanning. Opinions differ in the community on whether high contrast suits men; one thread argues contrast is overrated for male faces.

angle.text: Coloring maxxing changes how the face reads through tone and colour, using grooming, skincare, makeup, hair colour and clothing. Practitioners report that the effects show up in photos and in person quickly.

lead: Coloring maxxing (also coloringmaxxing, or the coloring guide) is a looksmaxxing framework about how the colours and tonal contrasts of the face combine into an overall impression. Its central claim is that well-defined contrast between the eyes, brows, lashes, teeth, lips, skin and hair makes a face look sharper, more alert and healthier, while low contrast makes even well-structured features look soft or flat [1].

People who follow it improve their appearance through colour and tone rather than bone structure: brighter teeth and sclera, even skin, defined brows and lashes, a considered hair colour and clothing that complements the complexion [1][2]. Because many of these steps are grooming or cosmetic, they are often described as among the quickest changes available.

Parts of the idea overlap with perception research on facial contrast and with seasonal colour analysis, a fashion and styling tradition. Forum guides add their own typologies and rules of thumb, such as darker hair than eyes counting as good contrast, which have not been formally tested [3][2].
infobox: Skin, hair, brows, lashes, eyes, teeth, lips
Seasonal color analysis; facial contrast research

paras: The framework looks at the face as an arrangement of light and dark regions. A widely shared forum guide describes facial contrast as the differences between the light and dark elements of the face and lists the eyes, teeth, eyebrows, hair and skin as the contributors [1]. It says clear sclera make the iris stand out and give a more alert look, while dull or darkened sclera make the face look tired [1].

A longer community guide titled the coloring guide covers why coloring matters, principles of ideal coloring, colouring types with the colours said to suit each, and ways to improve coloring [2]. Other threads concentrate on narrower topics: eyebrow and eyelash colouring [4], white teeth and sclera as a quick contrast gain [5], skin complexion [6], choosing a BB cream shade for face colour [7], and using clothing to create contrast [8].

The term circulates mainly on looksmax.org, where guides by members have been revised over time; the author of one popular guide says it is a remastered version of an earlier thread and calls the first attempt incomplete [2]. Threads such as a teaser for coloringmaxxing and posts claiming coloring and hair account for a large share of looks appear in the same community [9][10].

Members commonly state that a hair colour darker than the eyes is a good rule of thumb for contrast, and one thread contrasts examples of faces said to have high and low contrast [3]. Some posters argue that fair skin is the most preferred complexion by women [11]. Other members dispute the weight put on contrast: one thread argues that contrast is a poor strategy for men and questions why it is promoted [12].

Described in general terms, forum guides group actions into teeth whitening, eye brightening, brow and lash shaping or tinting, skin evenness and tone, hair colour and clothing choices [1][4][5][8]. Skin-focused threads cover complexion and shade-matching of base products [6][7][13].

Researchers at Bangor and Swansea examined facial contrast in a large set of faces and reported that women have higher eye contrast and lower brow contrast than men, that cosmetics amplify these sex-linked contrasts, and that makeup also boosts contrasts that fade with age [14]. Earlier work by Richard Russell reported that increasing the contrast of eyes and mouth raised attractiveness ratings for female faces but lowered them for male faces, a finding the forum debate about men and contrast echoes [12][14].

Seasonal color analysis, the styling tradition of matching clothing colours to skin, hair and eye colour, dates to the nineteenth century colour theory and was popularised by books such as Carole Jackson's Color Me Beautiful in 1980 [15]. A 2007 study cited on Wikipedia found inconsistencies between three seasonal systems, and the practice has no standard qualification [15].
No studies found on coloring maxxing as a framework. Related perception research on facial contrast is described above [14].
